brand.name: Glazed
brand.tagline: Seven in the case. Six smoothies. Seven sandwiches. Meet Savy on Harbor.
brand.welcomeScript: Hey! I'm Pip — welcome to Glazed. Today's case is seven: classic, coconut, cinnamon, chocolate, buttermilk, maple, and a bear claw. Six smoothies and seven sandwiches ride along. Flip a card, or ask me in chat.

shop.name: Savy Donuts & Smoothie
shop.address: 940 S Harbor Blvd, Santa Ana, CA 92704
shop.crossStreets: South Harbor near Kent — Anaheim / Santa Ana corridor
shop.cityNote: South Anaheim Harbor corridor (Santa Ana address)
shop.note: Neighborhood counter on South Harbor — fresh donuts, cold smoothies, and hot or cold subs from the deli. Look for the red SAVY DONUTS & SMOOTHIE sign, open neon, and the Fresh Donuts poster in the window. Come say hi; Pip’s stories live here too.

donuts.name: Classic Glazed
donuts.history: The ring doughnut’s origin story usually points to Rockport, Maine, where Captain Hanson Gregory said he punched out the soggy middle in 1847. Dutch olykoeks (“oil cakes”) had already arrived with New Amsterdam settlers, but the hole made frying even and created the American ring. By the early 1900s, automated doughnut machines and thin sugar glaze turned the shiny yeast ring into a breakfast staple from New York counters to West Coast shops — glaze sealing moisture so the crumb stays soft for hours.
donuts.avatarScript: Classic Glazed is the handshake of the donut world — yeast dough, hot oil, and a glassy vanilla coat.

origin.note: Captain Hanson Gregory claimed inventing the ring doughnut by knocking out the soggy center.

donuts.name: Coconut Glaze
donuts.history: Coconut on American doughnuts followed tropical trade and California–Hawaii bakery taste: a thin vanilla glaze rolled in shredded coconut so the ring stays shiny and the flake toasts at the edges. It is a West Coast case regular more than an Old World pastry — sunshine pantry on a yeast ring.
donuts.avatarScript: Coconut Glaze is a beach handshake — glassy vanilla and toasted flake crunch.

origin.note: Shredded coconut on a vanilla glaze — tropical pantry meeting the American yeast ring.

donuts.name: Cinnamon Glaze
donuts.tagline: Warm spice in a shiny coat
donuts.history: Cinnamon glaze folds warm spice into the sugar coat instead of a dry shake. The idea echoes spiced fried dough from Spanish and colonial kitchens, then American shops made a pourable cinnamon glaze that sets glossy and clings to a yeast ring.
donuts.avatarScript: Cinnamon Glaze is cozy shine — spice in the coat, not just dusted on top.

origin.note: Spice in the glaze, not only a sugar shake — bakery cousin to churros and warm fried dough.

donuts.name: Chocolate Glaze
donuts.tagline: Thin cocoa glass, not a frosting hat
donuts.history: Chocolate glaze is thinner than bakery frosting — cocoa, sugar, and a little fat that sets to a snap. American doughnut shops used it as a shiny cocoa dip, a quieter cousin of sprinkle-loaded chocolate frosted rings.
donuts.avatarScript: Chocolate Glaze is cocoa glass — a dip, a shine, no sprinkle party required.

origin.note: A thin cocoa dip that sets shiny — glaze energy, not a thick frosting crown.

donuts.name: Buttermilk
donuts.tagline: Tangy cake crumb, glaze in the cracks
donuts.history: Buttermilk cake doughnuts use tangy dairy and chemical leavening instead of yeast. The crumb fries dense and the surface cracks so glaze pools in every ridge — a Midwest and neighborhood-bakery staple, cousin to the sour-cream old-fashioned.
donuts.avatarScript: Buttermilk is the tangy cake ring — glaze hiding in every crack.

origin.note: Buttermilk cake rings — denser than yeast, built so glaze settles in the cracks.

donuts.name: Maple
donuts.history: Maple sugar and syrup are rooted in Indigenous foodways across the northeastern woodlands. Bakeries turned that forest sweetness into a maple glaze that sets amber on a warm ring — sugar-shack flavor without needing a walnut topping.
donuts.avatarScript: Maple is amber glaze — sticky forest sweet, no extra crunch required.

origin.note: Maple syrup has deep Indigenous roots; shops poured it as a cold-weather glaze.

donuts.name: Bear Claw
donuts.history: The bear claw is an American bakery pastry — yeast dough or Danish-style dough, almond paste or frangipane in the middle, and cuts along one edge that bake into “claws.” West Coast shops made it a case regular beside rings and fritters: not a punched hole, but still fryer-and-glaze family, with toasted almond perfume.
donuts.avatarScript: Bear Claw is the big paw of the case — almond heart and sugared toes.

origin.note: Almond-filled pastry with sliced “claws” — a West Coast bakery staple next to the doughnut case.

smoothies.name: Mango Sunrise

ingredients: ¾ cup orange juice or coconut milk
steps: Add liquid to reach a thick sip.
Pour cold and serve with a straw.

smoothies.history: Mango smoothies rode the 1990s–2000s juice-bar boom — ripe mango’s natural sweetness needs little sugar, so the drink stays bright and thick.
smoothies.avatarScript: Mango Sunrise is liquid sunshine — thick gold you can drink beside a warm donut.

smoothies.name: Berry Blast

ingredients: ¾ cup apple juice or milk
steps: Blend until smooth and vivid purple-red.
Taste for tartness; sweeten lightly if needed.

smoothies.history: Berry blends became smoothie-bar staples for color and punchy flavor — a tart counterpoint to sweet bakery cases.
smoothies.avatarScript: Berry Blast is the bold cup — deep berry color that wakes up the counter.

smoothies.name: Tropical Green

steps: Add fruit and blend until bright green.

smoothies.history: Green smoothies popularized veggies-in-a-cup in the 2010s — pineapple and banana keep spinach friendly for first-timers.
smoothies.avatarScript: Tropical Green is the sneaky healthy one — paradise flavor with a leafy wink.

smoothies.name: Strawberry Banana

steps: Pour and garnish with a berry if you like.

smoothies.history: Strawberry-banana is the gateway smoothie — soft fruit, familiar sweetness, and the drink most people order first at a donut-and-smoothie counter.
smoothies.avatarScript: Strawberry Banana is the classic handshake of the smoothie board — pink, creamy, forever.

smoothies.name: Cookies & Cream

ingredients: 2 cups vanilla ice cream or frozen yogurt
steps: Blend milk, ice cream, and vanilla until smooth.
Pulse in cookies so you still get crunchy bits.
Pour and top with cookie crumbs.

smoothies.history: Cookies-and-cream jumped from ice cream aisles into blender bars — a dessert cup that fits right beside a glazed donut case.
smoothies.avatarScript: Cookies & Cream is the dessert twin of the board — creamy, cookie-crunch, zero regrets.

smoothies.name: PB Banana Cocoa
smoothies.tagline: Peanut butter hug in a cup

steps: Taste for sweetness; add honey if needed.
Serve with a peanut-butter swirl if you’re feeling fancy.

smoothies.history: Peanut butter–banana drinks grew up in home kitchens and gyms, then landed on smoothie boards as the filling, savory-sweet option next to fruit cups.
smoothies.avatarScript: PB Banana Cocoa is the power hug — nutty, chocolatey, and perfect after a maple donut.

submarines.name: Italian Sub

steps: Split roll and drizzle with oil and vinegar.
Add lettuce, tomato, onion, and peppers.
Season with oregano, salt, and pepper.
Wrap tight and slice in half.

submarines.history: Italian subs descend from Italian-American deli culture — cold cuts, provolone, and vinegar-oil dressing on a long roll. The combo traveled from East Coast corner shops into national sandwich chains.
submarines.avatarScript: Italian Sub is the deli classic — layers of salami, provolone, and vinegar bite.

submarines.name: Turkey Club Sub

steps: Spread mayo and mustard on both sides.

submarines.history: The club sandwich — turkey, bacon, lettuce, tomato — was born in American social clubs in the late 1800s. Sub shops stretched it onto a long roll for a bigger, messier version.
submarines.avatarScript: Turkey Club Sub is the triple-stack hero — turkey, bacon, and toasted warmth.

submarines.name: Ham & Swiss
submarines.history: Ham and Swiss is the dependable lunch counter staple — no frills, just quality meat, good cheese, and a swipe of mustard.
submarines.avatarScript: Ham & Swiss is the quiet classic — dependable, mustard-kissed, always right.

submarines.name: Veggie Sub

steps: Split roll and drizzle with oil and vinegar.

submarines.history: Veggie subs rose alongside health-conscious eating in the 1980s–90s — proof that a sub doesn't need meat to be satisfying if the veggies are fresh and seasoned right.
submarines.avatarScript: Veggie Sub is the garden hero — crisp, bright, and a vinegar kick.

submarines.name: Meatball Sub

steps: Place meatballs in roll, spoon sauce over.
Top with cheese and melt under broiler.

submarines.history: Meatball subs are Italian-American comfort food — marinara, melted cheese, and soft bread soaking up every drop. A hot sub staple from corner delis to chains.
submarines.avatarScript: Meatball Sub is the messy winner — hot marinara, melted mozz, no napkin enough.

submarines.name: Tuna Salad Sub

steps: Mix tuna, mayo, mustard, celery, and onion.
Split roll and spread tuna salad.

submarines.history: Tuna salad subs are American lunch-counter heritage — canned tuna, mayo, and celery on a soft roll. Simple, filling, and a staple since mid-century diners.
submarines.avatarScript: Tuna Salad Sub is the retro champ — creamy, cold, and always lunch-ready.

submarines.name: Chicken Bacon Ranch
submarines.history: Chicken-bacon-ranch landed on American sandwich boards in the late 20th century as ranch dressing left the salad bowl. It is a deli and chain-sub staple — savory, creamy, and built for a toasted roll.
submarines.avatarScript: Chicken Bacon Ranch is the seventh sandwich — hot chicken, crisp bacon, cool ranch.
